record.title: MemCalib measures whether language-model agents give stored facts the right influence
record.summary: An October 8 v3 preprint introduces MemCalib, a benchmark that scores whether each fact in an agent’s stored memory should be ignored, used as bounded support, or allowed to control the answer. The authors report 15,000 examples across health, general assistance and coding. On its 1,500-example test set, the highest listed exact calibration is 28.40% for GPT-5.6-SOL; most evaluated models more often over-use memory than under-use it. The authors report that MemCalib-RL improves Qwen3-8B atom-use accuracy on this benchmark and transfers to a 150-query RPEval subset, while increasing under-use relative to the base model. Results are paper-reported and rely on constructed memory examples and rubric-guided model judging; real-world transfer is unknown.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The arXiv v3 paper defines atom-level memory-use targets (Ignore, Bound, Control) and reports a 15,000-example benchmark across health, general assistance and coding, with 13,500 training and 1,500 disjoint test examples. The authors describe the construction and evaluation protocol; the research desk did not independently audit the data.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On its 1,500-example test set, the paper reports low exact memory-use calibration across evaluated models; GPT-5.6-SOL has the highest listed Exact score at 28.40% (mean over three seeds). Most listed models show more severe/frequent over-use than under-use, while Qwen3-8B shows the reverse.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For Qwen3-8B on the paper’s test set, MemCalib-RL is reported to raise macro-averaged atom-use accuracy from 77.94% to 94.75% versus its cold-start comparator. On an external 150-query RPEval subset without additional training, it reports 33.78% macro and 78.12% micro accuracy over three seeds; under-use errors remain higher than the base model.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: These author-reported benchmark results do not establish that the metrics or training gains transfer to naturally occurring memory stores, other agent workloads, or deployment outcomes; independent reproduction was not inspected.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent execution of MemCalib or MemCalib-RL was performed; author-reported scores use rubric-guided LLM judging and three seeds.

MemCalib examples are constructed from eight public QA datasets with generated memory blocks, atom annotations and rubrics. Generalization to naturally accumulated, longitudinal agent memory is unknown.
The paper reports transfer to a 150-query RPEval subset, where all trained methods have higher under-use than the base model; broader transfer and false-omission costs remain unclear.

brief.importance_rationale: If the paper’s results generalize, evaluating each stored fact by how strongly it should influence a response could expose a memory-use failure that retrieval accuracy misses, and its reported training objective could improve agent-memory behavior. Current evidence is a single team’s constructed benchmark and judge-scored experiments, so cross-workload impact remains unestablished.
limitations: Single author-team preprint; no independent reproduction was inspected.
Benchmark examples are constructed from public QA datasets and generated/annotated memory atoms; real longitudinal memory is not tested.
Actual use-level judgments rely on rubric-guided LLM-as-a-Judge; the paper reports 96.7% agreement on 150 sampled judgments, with disagreements concentrated at the Bound/Control boundary.
Reported model results are averaged over three seeds; external RPEval transfer covers a 150-query subset and retains a higher under-use rate than the base model.

relationships.summary: Both assess how agents use retrieved memory; MemCalib measures atom-level influence while the related work adds a trust/action gate.

brief.summary: An October 8 v3 preprint introduces MemCalib, a benchmark that scores whether each fact in an agent’s stored memory should be ignored, used as bounded support, or allowed to control the answer. The authors report 15,000 examples across health, general assistance and coding. On its 1,500-example test set, the highest listed exact calibration is 28.40% for GPT-5.6-SOL; most evaluated models more often over-use memory than under-use it. The authors report that MemCalib-RL improves Qwen3-8B atom-use accuracy on this benchmark and transfers to a 150-query RPEval subset, while increasing under-use relative to the base model. Results are paper-reported and rely on constructed memory examples and rubric-guided model judging; real-world transfer is unknown.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report that MemCalib-RL improves Qwen3-8B macro-averaged atom-use accuracy from 77.94% to 94.75% on MemCalib test feedback, and obtains 33.78% macro / 78.12% micro accuracy on a 150-query RPEval subset without additional training. They also report higher under-use than the untrained base on RPEval.
technical.compute_or_cost: No end-to-end inference latency or deployment cost result is claimed in the reviewed paper sections.
technical.demonstrated_result: The v3 preprint and linked dataset card specify a benchmark of 15,000 examples, target memory-use labels and scoring definitions. This review inspected paper tables and dataset metadata but did not execute the evaluation or sample dataset rows.
technical.mechanism: Each memory atom receives a target influence level—Ignore, Bound or Control. MemCalib compares the target against a rubric-judged actual influence to measure over-use and under-use separately. MemCalib-RL decomposes target/actual pairs into reward channels and localizes counterfactual credit using atom ablation and response-token likelihood differences.
technical.regime: The authors construct 15,000 examples from eight public QA datasets in health, general assistance and coding. Baseline models are evaluated on 1,500 held-out examples, non-thinking mode, three seeds, temperature and top-p 1, with DeepSeek-V4-Pro judging. RPEval transfer uses 150 explicit multi-preference queries and three seeds.
technical.reproducibility: The authors link an implementation and dataset. This activation inspected the repository and dataset descriptions but did not run code or validate all source-data licenses.
technical.strongest_baseline: For the reported Qwen3-8B training comparison, the paper’s cold-start version of the same model is the direct comparator; for external transfer, the untrained base and several trained optimization methods are compared under the RPEval protocol.

brief.title: MemCalib measures whether language-model agents give stored facts the right influence
brief.why_it_matters: Memory systems can retrieve a relevant fact yet still give it too much or too little influence. MemCalib’s item-level Ignore/Bound/Control labels make that behavior measurable and distinguish over-use from under-use. The authors report gains from a training method on their benchmark and a small external subset, but the examples are constructed and the judges are models; deployment performance is not established.

related.summary: Both assess how agents use retrieved memory; MemCalib measures atom-level influence while the related work adds a trust/action gate.

other.title: A preprint tests a lightweight trust gate for conflicting memories in language-model agents
other.summary: An arXiv v1 preprint proposes the Memory Decision Layer, a zero-trained-parameter controller that evaluates retrieved memories before generation using relevance, reliability and task risk, then chooses whether to adopt or abstain. In benchmark experiments with constructed memory conflicts, the authors report lower hallucination rates than standard retrieval-augmented generation in tested settings, including zero hallucinations in the tested high-risk samples for several models. On one Gemma TruthfulQA comparison, MDL and standard RAG both had 4.8% overall hallucination, while high-risk rates were 0.0% and 11.9%, respectively. The paper reports about 0.14 ms added latency when embeddings are precomputed, but also residual active-action errors. These are single-team paper results, not independent confirmation or evidence of production performance.
